s.g: The infinitive suffix for many verbs. Usually indicates an imperfective verb. Often used to derive imperfective verbs from prefixed perfective verbs in -ить (-itʹ), and triggers iotation.
x: на- (na-) + пра́вить impf (právitʹ, “to drive, to steer”) → напра́вить pf (naprávitʹ, “to direct”) + -я́ть (-játʹ) → направля́ть impf (napravljátʹ)

s.g: auto da fe (public announcement of the sentences imposed by the Inquisition on supposed heretics; public execution by burning at the stake)

ety.text: Per Russian language dictionary (1897), ево́йный (jevójnyj) is from ево́ный (jevónyj, “his”) with 'й' from е́йный (jéjnyj). Compare Old Polish jegojski and Russian ево́й (jevój) and свой (svoj), твой (tvoj), мой (moj).

Borrowed from Dutch kwitantie, see there for more. Compare Italian quietanza.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin magister. Doublet of ма́стер (máster), маэ́стро (maéstro), ми́стер (míster), and мэтр (mɛtr). From the Latin source the second component of гроссме́йстер (grossméjster) is also derived. Also note a coordinate Latin term minister (whence мини́стр (minístr)).

s.g: monorail (a railroad system where the trains run on one rail; a train running on a single rail)

ety.text: From пе́чь (péčʹ, “to bake”) + -е́нье (-énʹje), from Proto-Slavic *peťì, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *pektei, from Proto-Indo-European *pékʷeti, from the root *pekʷ-, whence English cook and biscuit (in part).

Via Middle Russian, then probably borrowed Old Pskovian *полꙑмѧ (*polymę), from Proto-Slavic *pòlmy. Cognate with Belarusian по́лымя (pólymja). Doublet of пла́мя (plámja) and по́ломя (pólomja), where the first one is an Old Church Slavonic word showing liquid metathesis characteristic of South Slavic area, and the second one normally inherited by pleophony of *TorT > *ToroT type, while Old Pskovian dialect (Krivichs area) reflex of pleophony *TolT > *TolᵊT, *TolᵒT.

s.g: to guess, to get to the core, to get to the heart, to get to the bottom (of), to see through (someone), to get (someone's) measure

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *Svętovitъ (“holy lord”), made of Proto-Slavic *svętъ (“holy”) and Proto-Slavic *vitъ (“lord”). Corresponds to Polish Świętowit.
